# Basics of R

## What is R? Why should I use R?

Available at www.r-project.org

* Free statistical environment for interactive use
* Interpreted, functional scripting/programming language - you type in, you see output
* Descends from the S language, written by statisticians for statisticians

## What can you do with R?

::: {.fragment}
Anything!
:::

::: {.fragment}
* Do calculations
* Write functions
* Analyse data. ALL the data. Well, almost. But really, almost.
* Apply advanced statistical techniques
* Do beautiful & publication-ready plots
* Develop interactive web-applications
* Presentations & documents (this one)
:::

## Why should I use R?

::: {.fragment}
* It works! And it is quite powerful
* It is free, open-source, and available for all OS
* You can really do whatever you might aim to do in terms of statistics
* It offers awesome possibilities for (interactive) graphing
* It has a wide, active and competent community (ok, communities: statistics, bioinformatics, machine learning, …)
* It can be extended with packages. More power!
* Escape Point-and-Click-land, you work with syntax: you can use, re-use elements, validate & reproduce analysis
:::

## Why should I not use R?

::: {.fragment}
* You use it or lose it
* The learning curve might be steep
* Can be frustrating if you have errors
* Help might be available, but it is sometimes very technical
* Many packages, a blessing and a curse: how, how good
:::

# Using R within an IDE

## Get R - and RStudio

::: {.fragment}
* Go to https://www.r-project.org/ and get the latest version
* Go to https://posit.co/products/open-source/rstudio and download RStudio
:::

::: {.fragment}
Alternatives:

* Positron (https://positron.posit.co/download.html)
* Microsoft VS Code (https://code.visualstudio.com/)
* OpenAnalytics Architect (https://www.getarchitect.io/)
:::

## First ride: look around you

::: {.fragment}
You'll have…

* The Console (command prompt)
* The Source Editor (write your code here - and then run it)
* The Environment (an overview of the created objects)
* The History (your previous commands)
* Files browser
* Plots viewer
* Help viewer
* Data viewer
* Package viewer
* Your Working Directory for the R session
:::

## A good IDE will give you...

* Ways to open/load/save files
* The possibility to run commands from the editor
* A good syntax highlighting
* Suggested completions (for functions, arguments, objects, ...) - TAB is your friend
* Some diagnostics on your code

## Do these things now, thank me later

* Global options - start always from the scratch!
  - Do not restore .Rdata at startup
  - Never save workspace on exit
  
* Use the maximum real estate space for your code/editor
  - Put the console on the right + maximize the editor

* Have a theme that could be gentle on your eyes (Solarized light, but you do you) - this can also help you for the syntax highlighting

* Work as a project - .Rproj files are your friend

* Spend some time having a look at the menus above. They contain an amazing/awful lot of things and useful functions

* Get some familiarity with keyboard shortcuts!

# R documentation

## `r emo::ji("notes")` Help! `r emo::ji("notes")`

```{r}
#| eval: false
## this calls the help for a function to plot a histogram
?hist
# this is just the same
help(hist) ## what about ??
```

::: {.fragment}
Check out what these do

```{r}
#| eval: false
?apropos
apropos("row")
??row
```
:::

## Where do I look for help?

- Integrated help system, with executable examples
- (for some packages) Vignettes (typical problem, commands, and workflow)
- CRAN Task Views: https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/
- Books! (I will put together an opinionated list at the end...)
- Courses!
- Online: mailing lists, forums (StackOverflow, ...), blogs, Twitter (`#rstats`)
- LLMs - use them with judgement!!!


## Make your life easier - Take notes for your future self

::: {.fragment}
- Add comments and document your own code

```{r}
# This is a comment
```

- write clean code - use spaces, indentation
- use an editor with syntax highlighting/some form of autocompletion 
:::

::: {.fragment}
Careful here:

- R is case sensitive and has zero-tolerance with mis-spelled names
- Parentheses: open *and* close them
- Special attention with missing values, factors VS strings: R is clever, but you might think differently
- Do not be stingy with parentheses - if this helps you
- Same goes with comments - your colleagues and your future self will thank you
:::

# A project, in/with R

## What's a good project?

Goes a bit with the Anna Karenina principle...

::: {.fragment}
Some foundations:

* Use RStudio projects, "think project-wise": imagine to carry along the (relevant part of the) universe with you
* Think of a useful folder structure for your future data and programs (literally, any. Any that works for you)
* Use names that are representative of their function - and be consistent
* Leave your mental breadcrumbs in - use comments, put them up on top
:::

## Useful folder structure

::: {.fragment}
* It helps to navigate even complex projects
* You quickly grasp the purpose of your older programs 
* You have colleagues, friends, reviewers: Help others to navigate your work!
:::

::: {.fragment}
The work you invest now WILL overall reduce your required work in the long run, pinky swear!

Have main folders, create separate sub-folders for Data, Documents, generated figures...
:::

## Naming things

... is a lost art. Do master that art. 

Don't call your data `mydata`.

Possibly: don't use spaces in the names, use underscores or dashes

::: {.fragment}
A good example:

`[Project name]_[Optional number]_[Short descriptive name]_[Version].[extension]`

Why is this good?

Keep it simple for now

`[Lecture name]_[Exercise name or description].[extension]`
:::

## Use comments/text

... to leave essential infos in

Feel free and invited to do at the top of the files

An informative header should be the start of every file you use (we will see soon how this can work out)

Who's going to love this?

## Who knows RMarkdown?

::: {.fragment}
R Markdown allows you to create documents that serve as a neat record of your analysis. 

Why?

- We want other researchers to easily understand what we did in our analysis, otherwise nobody can be certain that you analysed your data properly (yay, reproducible research!)
- Create an R markdown document as an appendix to a paper or project assignment, upload it to an online repository such as Github, or simply to keep as a personal record (*future you* will thank *present you* for this)
:::

::: {.fragment}
The key point is...

R Markdown documents present your code alongside its output (graphs, tables, etc.) with conventional text to explain it, a bit like a notebook. To do this, R Markdown uses **markdown** syntax (that's the thing that is also used by LLMs when rendering the conversation, in case you ever copy-pasted from these...). 
:::

## Now there is Quarto!

https://quarto.org/

Quarto is a multi-language, next generation version of R Markdown (also from Posit), with many new features and capabilities

::: {.fragment}
The price to pay on top to have an Rmd/qmd document is sooooo small - and for that, you get

- Code, text, output all together
- One file only - no need to get lost among many output items
- It even looks nice
- It can be rendered to many formats

If you have installed a recent enough version of RStudio, you might be all set already!
:::

## Let's create one Quarto document together!

... and use it throughout this WHOLE COURSE.

::: {.fragment}
To create a new Quarto file (`.qmd`), select `File -> New File -> Quarto document...` in RStudio

The newly created `.qmd` file comes with basic instructions 
:::

::: {.fragment}
The different parts of it:

- An (optional) YAML header surrounded by `---`s
- R code chunks surrounded by backticks (```)
- text mixed with simple text formatting

Let's insert text and code - any text, any code
:::

## Code comes in chunks

... and chunks have options to control the behavior/the output of each

Detailed very nicely here: https://quarto.org/docs/computations/r.html#code-blocks

::: {.fragment}
Some useful ones: 

* `label`
* `echo`
* `eval`
* `results`
* `fig.height` & co
:::

## Rendering a document

When a Quarto document is rendered, ALL R code blocks are automatically executed (top to bottom). 

You can render Quarto documents e.g. using the Render button

::: {.fragment}
